children: Wall Street closed higher Friday as easing Treasury yields and lower oil prices supported equities, with investors continuing to monitor developments surrounding the Strait of Hormuz.
The blue-chip Dow
was up 0.9%, the benchmark S&P 500 (
) advanced 0.5%, and the tech-focused Nasdaq Composite
gained 0.4%.
The S&P 500 gained 1.22% for the week.
Seeking Alpha analyst
was surprised by how resilient the markets have been this week.

He argued that the obstacles were not insignificant; we saw Treasury yields continue to rise, with the 30-year bond even returning to its highest levels in over twenty years. Additionally, weaker-than-usual demand was evident in both 5- and 7-year auction results, particularly from foreign investors, which is a concern. Although there would be continuous treasury demand, the yield would rise because of the risk premium. Geopolitically, oil still was a problem, with prices fluctuating from $97 to $108.

“Despite all these negative catalysts, the market remained positive. Among the reasons was certainly the strength of the AI and software sectors, whose flame was rekindled with the arrival of Muse, which has dragged the tech sector back to the forefront,” Agar Capital concluded.
From a sector-level perspective, four S&P sectors ended the week in positive territory, while seven sectors finished in the red.
Technology
and Communication Services
were the strongest-performing sectors this week, with gains of 3.59% and 1.93%, respectively.
Seeking Alpha analyst
said that we got another week with tech and communication services up, mostly big tech and software.

However, he warned that a lot of this has to do with the narrowing of the market, and we can see that narrowness in the performance. Big tech hyperscalers are up, but everything else seems down or flat. That narrowness is usually not a good sign, and so bulls should be cautious here, even as tech gains.
Conversely, Utilities
and Energy
posted the weakest weekly performances, falling 3.82% and 3.56%, respectively.

Bowman concluded, “With all the talk about how much power AI needs, it's interesting to see utilities and energy at the bottom of the list this week. That makes sense to me because of where yields are headed. These sectors are highly correlated with duration and inflation expectations. Given how volatile fuel pricing and diesel have been, I expect that the losses won't stop here for utilities and energy. If the 10-year yield stabilizes, maybe we'll see some softness in utilities because of its duration exposure. That said, it's unclear to me what catalyst would cause the 10-year to stop moving up at this point.”
